summary: Describes properties of and relationships among Real-time Transport Protocol sources, both existing and proposed, and defines common terminology for discussing them, since the terms can be complex and confusing.

eli5.summary: This is a dictionary that explains who is who in a group video call.

questions: what is the terminology for rtp sources
what is the difference between an rtp stream and an rtp session
what do srst and mrmt mean
subtitle: A shared vocabulary for the pipeline a media source goes through in RTP, and for how streams, sessions and participants relate.

tldr.problem: Terms for Real-time Transport Protocol (RTP) sources are confusing and inconsistent: different protocols reuse the same words for different things, and complexity handled at one layer is often ignored at another.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC models media as a chain of streams and transformations from physical stimulus to rendered output, defines the communication entities around it (endpoint, RTP session, participant and so on), and then maps existing terms onto that model.
tldr.outcome: It is a terminology and concepts document, not a protocol. It adds no new security considerations beyond those of RTP itself.

facts.label: Media transport identifier
facts.value: 5-tuple (source address, source port, destination address, destination port, protocol)

today: RFC 7656 is an Informational RFC and no later RFC is recorded as obsoleting or updating it. It remains a vocabulary reference rather than a protocol specification.

sections.title: The Terminology Problem
sections.content:
The taxonomy of sources in RTP (RFC 3550) has been regarded as confusing and inconsistent. Two frequently cited examples are that protocols using RTP use the same terms to mean different things, and that complexity solved at one layer is glossed over at another.

RFC 7656 clears this up by describing how RTP sources are transformed between sender and receiver, and how they can be grouped and associated. For each concept it lists alternate definitions that exist today and characteristics that describe it. References to CLUE mean the telepresence framework, and references to WebRTC mean its overview document.
sections.eli5: People kept using the same word for different things, like calling both a pizza and a slice a pizza. This document picks clear names.

sections.title: The Media Chain
sections.content:
Media is a sequence of physical stimuli (sound waves, photons, key strokes) in digital form. The model has two kinds of things: streams, which are time-based sequences of samples in some representation, and transformations, which change the representation. A transformation may have zero or more inputs and one or more outputs, and if one output feeds several inputs the streams are identical.

On the sender side the chain runs: media capture produces a raw stream; a media source (synchronized to a reference clock) produces a source stream; a media encoder produces an encoded stream; a media packetizer produces a source RTP stream. Optional RTP-based redundancy produces a redundancy RTP stream, and optional RTP-based security (such as SRTP) produces a secured RTP stream before it enters the media transport.

The receiver side mirrors this with validation, repair, depacketizing, decoding, a media sink and a media render. Streams coming out of reverse steps are prefixed with received because they may differ from what was sent, for example because of lossy coding or packet loss that repair could not fix.

The media transport is itself broken down into a sender, a network transport (which may cause loss, delay, duplication and corruption) and a receiver. The RFC stresses that this is a conceptual model, and real implementations may be structured differently.
sections.eli5: Think of a game of telephone with a machine at each step. A camera captures, a packer boxes things up, the network carries the boxes and may lose some, and at the other end the boxes are unpacked and shown on a screen.

sections.title: RTP Streams, Sessions and Participants
sections.content:
An RTP stream is a stream of RTP packets with media data, identified by an SSRC in a particular RTP session. A stream has one SSRC at a time, but the SSRC can change, for example after an SSRC collision or a clock rate change. Each SSRC defines its own sequence numbering and timing space, and several RTP streams can represent a single media source.

The entities around the chain are:

  • Endpoint: a single addressable entity sending or receiving RTP packets. It belongs to at most one participant at a time.
  • RTP session: a group communications channel that can carry a number of RTP streams, sharing one SSRC space and the RTCP bandwidth.
  • Participant: an entity reachable by a single signaling address, such as a SIP URI.
  • Multimedia session: an association among participants using one or more RTP sessions.
  • Communication session: an association among two or more participants via one or more multimedia sessions.

Each media transport contains only one RTP session, while one RTP session can span several media transports. A media transport is normally identified by a 5-tuple of source address, source port, destination address, destination port and transport protocol.
sections.eli5: A call is like a school trip. The trip is the communication session, each kid is a participant, each kid's backpack is an endpoint, and each walkie-talkie channel is an RTP session carrying many voices.

sections.title: How Streams Relate to Each Other
sections.content:
Section 3 of the RFC looks at the relationships that applications must track. A synchronization context is a requirement for a strong timing relationship between media sources. It can be identified by the RTCP CNAME, by clock source signaling in SDP, implicitly through a WebRTC media stream, or explicitly through SDP grouping such as Lip Synchronization.

Patterns it describes include:

  • Simulcast: one media source encoded into several independent encoded streams.
  • Layered multi-stream: a scalable encoding sent as separate RTP streams. The RFC defines the shorthand SRST (single RTP stream on a single media transport), MRST (multiple RTP streams on a single media transport) and MRMT (multiple RTP streams on multiple media transports).
  • RTP stream duplication, a redundancy method that sends the same stream more than once, optionally delayed.
  • RTP retransmission and forward error correction, where a redundancy RTP stream must be tied back to its source RTP stream.

Related streams can be separated by SSRC alone within one RTP session, or placed in different RTP sessions. The RFC also notes a proposal to carry several RTP sessions over one media transport, which means a 5-tuple alone no longer tells you which RTP session a stream belongs to.
sections.eli5: Sometimes the same video is sent in a big, medium and small version, or a spare copy is sent in case one gets lost. The receiver needs labels to know which pieces belong together.

sections.title: Mapping Existing Terms
sections.content:
Section 4 maps terms from other specifications onto the model. For CLUE telepresence it covers terms such as Capture Device (a physical entity doing media capture), Capture Encoding (an encoded stream) and Stream (an RTP stream). For WebRTC, an RtcMediaStream is a set of media sources sharing one synchronization context and an RtcMediaStreamTrack is a media source.

It also clarifies ambiguous terms from SVC (RFC 6190): Multi-Session Transmission corresponds to MRST or MRMT, and Single-Session Transmission closely corresponds to SRST. A Multipoint Control Unit is described as including one participant and one or more related endpoints. The RFC also notes that in RFC 3550 the SSRC acts both as an identifier for an encoded stream and, in effect, as a name for a media packetizer.
sections.eli5: This part is a translation table. It says: when team A says one word and team B says another, here is how they line up in our dictionary.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The document aims to reduce confusion caused by inconsistent use of RTP terms. It does not introduce new security considerations beyond those of RTP (RFC 3550) and of the protocols that use it. The authors argue that a well-defined common terminology helps lead to better standards and so avoids security problems.

Within the model itself, RTP-based security such as SRTP is a transformation that can apply authentication, integrity protection and confidentiality. The RFC notes that in SRTP all of these are optional except integrity protection of SRTCP, which is mandatory, and that when redundancy is added to an already secured stream the redundancy stream still needs authentication and integrity protection.
sections.eli5: A dictionary does not open any new doors for burglars. The locks are the same ones that RTP already uses.

layers.label: Media Capture
layers.detail: Physical stimulus becomes a raw stream

layers.label: Media Source
layers.detail: Raw stream becomes a source stream, tied to a reference clock

layers.label: Media Encoder
layers.detail: Source stream becomes an encoded stream

layers.label: Media Packetizer
layers.detail: Encoded stream becomes a source RTP stream

layers.label: RTP-Based Security
layers.detail: Optional: produces a secured RTP stream

layers.label: Media Transport
layers.detail: Sends the stream towards the receiver

items.title: SRST
items.text: Single RTP stream on a single media transport.

items.title: MRST
items.text: Multiple RTP streams on a single media transport.

items.title: MRMT
items.text: Multiple RTP streams on multiple media transports.
